questions.question: An arm scores 0/40. Why report the Wilson interval instead of the naive p ± 1.96·√(p(1−p)/n)?

answerOptions.text: The naive interval collapses to zero width at 0/40, falsely claiming certainty; Wilson gives an honest asymmetric upper bound inside [0,1]
answerOptions.rationale: At p=0 the naive half-width is 0, so it 'proves' 0% from 40 trials. Wilson stays in [0,1] and yields a real upper bound (about 8.8%).

answerOptions.text: Wilson is centered exactly on the observed proportion, which the naive interval is not
answerOptions.rationale: Backwards — Wilson is deliberately not centered on p (it shrinks toward 0.5 at small N); that asymmetry is the honesty.

answerOptions.text: The naive interval requires an LLM judge to compute
answerOptions.rationale: Neither interval involves a judge; this confuses the statistics step with the grading step.

answerOptions.text: Wilson needs no sample size, so it works when N is unknown
answerOptions.rationale: Wilson very much uses N; the point is it behaves well at small N, not that N is optional.

questions.hint: Think about the width of the naive interval when p is exactly 0.

questions.question: A gap between two arms has a Newcombe 95% interval of [−0.02, +0.10]. How should it be reported?

answerOptions.text: As a null — the interval includes zero, so the gap is indistinguishable from no effect
answerOptions.rationale: The portfolio's rule: a difference whose interval contains zero is reported as a null, not spun as a trend.

answerOptions.text: As a +10 percentage-point effect, using the upper bound
answerOptions.rationale: Cherry-picking the upper bound ignores that the interval also covers zero and negatives.

answerOptions.text: As a real effect, since most of the interval is positive
answerOptions.rationale: 'Mostly positive' is exactly the spin pre-registration forbids; containing zero means null.

answerOptions.text: As invalid, because Newcombe cannot be used on a difference
answerOptions.rationale: Newcombe is the correct tool for a difference of proportions; it is not invalid here.

questions.hint: What is the single decision rule for a difference interval?

questions.question: Why compute a Newcombe interval for the gap rather than subtracting the two arms' Wilson intervals?

answerOptions.text: Subtracting two intervals mishandles the combined uncertainty of a difference; Newcombe is built for it
answerOptions.rationale: The uncertainty of a difference is not the naive combination of two single-proportion intervals; Newcombe accounts for it.

answerOptions.text: Wilson intervals cannot be computed for treatment arms
answerOptions.rationale: Wilson applies to any single proportion, treatment or baseline.

answerOptions.text: Newcombe is just Wilson with a bigger z, so it is always wider
answerOptions.rationale: Newcombe is not 'Wilson with a bigger z'; it is a method for the difference.

answerOptions.text: Because two overlapping Wilson intervals always mean a real effect
answerOptions.rationale: Overlap (or not) of single-arm intervals does not by itself determine whether the gap excludes zero.

questions.hint: The quantity you care about is a difference, not two separate proportions.

questions.question: What does pre-registration concretely guarantee in these projects?

answerOptions.text: The scoring script and pass bar are frozen before paid data exists, and the verdict exits INVALID on wrong-arm input
answerOptions.rationale: Committing the gate as code before data removes goalpost-moving — the core reason a null here is credible.

answerOptions.text: That the result will be statistically significant
answerOptions.rationale: Pre-registration makes results honest, not significant; it often produces pre-committed nulls.

answerOptions.text: That an LLM judge approved the rubric in advance
answerOptions.rationale: No LLM judge is involved; the gate is deterministic code.

answerOptions.text: That the budget cap will not be exceeded
answerOptions.rationale: That is the budget guard, a separate mechanism from pre-registering the statistics.

questions.hint: It is about when the verdict logic is written relative to the data.

questions.question: Why grade with a deterministic oracle (exact-match / token-ownership) instead of an LLM judge?

answerOptions.text: A deterministic checker is reproducible and cannot be sweet-talked; you trade subtlety for a verdict any skeptic can re-run
answerOptions.rationale: Judge-free grading sidesteps the self-graded-homework trap — the checker gives everyone the same answer.

answerOptions.text: An LLM judge is too slow to run at hobby scale
answerOptions.rationale: Speed is not the issue; credibility and reproducibility are.

answerOptions.text: Deterministic oracles capture nuance an LLM judge would miss
answerOptions.rationale: It is the opposite — you give up nuance to buy reproducibility.

answerOptions.text: Because Wilson intervals require an oracle to compute
answerOptions.rationale: The interval math is independent of how you grade pass/fail.

questions.hint: Which grader can a hostile reviewer reproduce exactly?

questions.question: A skeptic asks how you keep the claim that these run 'cheap' honest. What is the concrete answer?

answerOptions.text: A hard budget guard tracks spend to the cent against a fixed cap and stops the run — e.g. ghost-patch closed for $1.42
answerOptions.rationale: 'Cheap' is a controlled claim backed by a tracked, committed spend ledger, not a vague intention.

answerOptions.text: The models are free, so cost is never a concern
answerOptions.rationale: They are paid OpenRouter calls; the guard is what bounds the cost.

answerOptions.text: Costs are estimated afterward from the number of runs
answerOptions.rationale: Spend is tracked live to the cent against a cap, not back-estimated.

answerOptions.text: The budget is enforced by the LLM judge
answerOptions.rationale: There is no LLM judge, and grading is unrelated to spend tracking.

questions.hint: There is a committed ledger and a hard cap.
